detail.title: Learning from Editorial Decisions: Optimizing Audience-Wide Content Promotions with Causal Machine Learning

detail.abstract: Marketing decisions that once relied on expert judgment are increasingly informed by data and models. One prominent application is the audience-wide promotion problem faced by content publishers (e.g., newspapers, magazines, independent producers), who sequentially over time select a few items out of many to promote uniformly to their audience based on rich past information. In this paper, we consider the objective of using data from such expert decisions to learn new decision policies that improve upon them. To this end, we collaborate with a leading Swiss newspaper and use six weeks of high-frequency panel data that record all editorial choices, all information shown to editors at decision time, and all outcomes from their decisions. Informed by the setting, we frame the editorial decision process as a contextual bandit with selection bias but strong variation across contexts and treatments. We combine this framing with causal machine learning methods to learn conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) of promotion and evaluate counterfactual policies. In our application, we find that editors act "as if" they optimize for the CATE of their promotion decisions and associated uncertainty, yet implementing counterfactual policies that actually optimize for such objectives could have increased annual revenue by USD 0.28–1.41 million. Our study shows how causal machine learning can be applied to observational data on expert decisions to test what latent reward signals experts optimize for and, in turn, evaluate what gains machine-learned policies that optimize for such signals could bring.

title: The Unseen Connections: Link Prediction via Pattern Matching in Large Networks
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Computer Science, University of California, Irvine - Department of Computer Science,  and University of California, Irvine - Department of Computer Science

detail.title: The Unseen Connections: Link Prediction via Pattern Matching in Large Networks
detail.abstract: Link prediction is a key challenge across various network domains, from biology to social and technological systems. Existing link prediction methods fall short in one or more of the following ways: they may require node attributes, making them domain specific and inapplicable to arbitrary networks; they may use sophisticated methods like matrix factorization or graph embeddings that work well on small networks but fail to scale; or they use simple predictors like common neighbors or Jaccard similarity that, while scalable, fail to account for higher-order patterns and simply don’t work on large, real-world networks. In this work, we introduce BLANT-Predict: a scalable link prediction framework that uses network topology alone—specifically, higher-order graphlet patterns—making it applicable to arbitrary networks. We compare our approach against 13 state-of-the-art methods on 12 real-world networks with up to a million nodes and 3 million edges. We find that BLANT-Predict outperforms them all, both in precision and scalability. Finally in addition to the common approach of k-fold cross-validation, we apply a novel evaluation framework we call “time travel” that more closely mimics the real-world situation: we make predictions “about the future” using only data available as of time T1, and evaluate them using data from a later date T2. We find that BLANT-Predict almost universally outperforms other methods in these tests, demonstrating its usefulness in the real-world scenario of predicting future, as-yet-unobserved data.

title: BootKitty: A Critical Analysis of Modern Bootkit-Rootkit Threats and Defense Limitations in Contemporary Cybersecurity Infrastructure

detail.title: BootKitty: A Critical Analysis of Modern Bootkit-Rootkit Threats and Defense Limitations in Contemporary Cybersecurity Infrastructure
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of BootKitty, a sophisticated proof-of-concept bootkit and rootkit that exemplifies the evolving landscape of firmware-level threats in modern computing environments. Unlike traditional malware that exploits software vulnerabilities, BootKitty targets the fundamental trust model of the boot process itself, operating at a level that renders conventional security controls ineffective. Through examination of recent case studies, including the Ivanti Connect Secure breach, this research demonstrates that bootkit tactics have transitioned from theoretical concerns to operational threats in real-world attack scenarios. The paper evaluates existing mitigation strategies, including Secure Boot, Trusted Platform Module (TPM)-based attestation, and measured boot validation, while highlighting the significant implementation gaps in critical infrastructure environments. Our analysis reveals that effective defense against such threats requires a paradigm shift toward hardware-rooted trust and firmware integrity verification, challenging the traditional software-centric approach to cybersecurity. This work contributes to the understanding of low-level persistent threats and provides recommendations for enhanced security architectures that address the limitations of current defensive strategies.

detail.abstract: Smart contracts are computer programs. Somewhat inexplicably, they are also contracts. Can computer programs be contracts? Can code be enforceable? Can contracts self-enforce or self-execute? Can programs execute contracts or automate the performance of contractual obligations? One moment: what exactly are smart contracts? What is the benefit of smart contracts being contracts in the legal sense? For something that is supposed to be a building block of the new crypto economy, there is surprisingly little consensus as to the meaning of the term. Popular narratives promise a decentralized future, where empowered individuals remain in control of their destiny and no longer require overpriced lawyers, evil bankers and corrupt judges. The theories surrounding smart contracts are captivating, indeed. The accompanying legal analyses, however, somewhat shallow. Glossing over inconsistent definitions and conveniently bypassing fundamental questions, legal scholars often seek refuge in tweet-sized one-liners. The new era of crypto-economy starts with a large doctrinal debt concerning the very nature of smart contracts and their role in contract law, if any. The problem is not purely academic in nature. The spate of recent regulations, enforcement actions and court orders reveal a deeply seated conceptual confusion surrounding both the technology and some fundamental legal concepts.

detail.abstract: European financial institutions face a distinctive challenge in operationalising DORA: transforming observability, incident governance and third-party control from compliance exercises into embedded elements of software delivery. The focus is practical. Observability is anchored in user-facing indicators and traceable records rather than tool catalogues, so that evidence read by engineers can also be followed by supervisors. Incident management is framed as real-time classification against regulatory thresholds with an auditable trail that shows who decided, on what basis and when notifications were sent. Third-party risk moves from periodic review to continuous dependency visibility, vendor-impact correlation and exercised exit strategies that prove substitutability. Two implementation archetypes recur in practice. Large banks advance by placing controls at legacy boundaries and migrating inward through bounded services while keeping external contracts stable. Mid-size and greenfield organisations adopt a platform-led model in which golden paths and asynchronous enforcement preserve speed without losing accountability. Across both contexts, two patterns explain most success: integration before tools, and automation measured by outcomes such as time to detect, time to recover and change failure rate. Limits are explicit. Results depend on disciplined evidence generation and on validating improvements across incidents rather than relying on narrative claims. The aim is lower compliance cost and resilience that customers can feel.

title: The Face and Future of Cyberthreats: Emerging Challenges and Trends
affiliations: University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, South Africa, University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, South Africa and University of Johannesburg, Johannesburg, South Africa

detail.title: The Face and Future of Cyberthreats: Emerging Challenges and Trends
detail.abstract: The cybersecurity landscape is rapidly evolving, driven by emerging technologies and increasingly sophisticated threats. This systematic literature review synthesizes challenges, defensive strategies, and sector-specific vulnerabilities identified across 52 scholarly sources published between 2015 and 2025. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning are highlighted as both critical threat vectors and promising defensive mechanisms, featuring in nearly half of the studies. Human factors, including skills gaps, human error, and training deficiencies, remain pervasive vulnerabilities, cited in over 35% of the literature. The review identifies finance, government, and healthcare as the most frequently impacted sectors, while emerging threats such as ransomware, supply chain attacks, and phishing continue to escalate. Geographically, research is concentrated in India and the USA, indicating potential limitations in the global generalizability of findings. Foundational strategies, including security frameworks, standards, and awareness programs, remain prominent in proposed mitigations. This review underscores the need for balanced attention to underrepresented threats and enhanced methodological transparency, providing an evidence-based foundation to guide researchers, industry stakeholders, and policymakers in developing proactive and resilient cybersecurity strategies. The cybersecurity landscape is rapidly evolving as emerging technologies expand attack surfaces and adversaries escalate in sophistication. To synthesize emerging challenges, sectoral impacts, and defensive trends in cybersecurity and identify evidence gaps. Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science; publications 2015-2025. Study eligibility criteria: Peer-reviewed, English-language studies addressing emerging cyberthreats or defensive paradigms, with an explicit research framework/methodology. Appraisal and synthesis methods: Independent dual/triple screening; data extraction by three reviewers with consensus; quality appraisal using JBI and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; narrative/thematic synthesis. 52 studies met criteria (journals 57.69%, conferences 25.00%). Research is geographically concentrated (India 23.08%, USA 21.15%). AI/ML appears as both threat and defence in ≈27-31% of studies; human factors are cited in ≥35%. Most-studied sectors: finance and government (each 13.46%); energy/health/transport (5.77% each). Common threats: AI/ML-driven attacks, industrial/critical-infrastructure risks, cloud/supply-chain compromise. Dominant defences: AI-driven detection/response, security hygiene, and training/awareness. Conceptual bias (limited empirical validation), sector/region skew, and potential reporting/selection bias. Evidence supports integrated, proactive cyber defence combining AI-enabled controls with governance and human-centred measures. Gaps include post-quantum preparedness, supply-chain resilience, and coverage of under-studied regions/sectors.

title: Compliance and Internal Controls: Standards and Practices in Cyber Security Governance

detail.title: Compliance and Internal Controls: Standards and Practices in Cyber Security Governance
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly confront challenges such as regulatory non-compliance, fragmented control mechanisms, and inconsistent monitoring processes. This systematic literature review evaluates the role of structured compliance standards and internal control frameworks in strengthening cybersecurity governance, audit readiness, and organizational resilience. Following a comprehensive search across Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus, eighty (n = 80) studies published between 2015 and 2025 were identified and analyzed through a structured screening and synthesis process. The review reveals that ISO 27001 (25%) and COBIT (24%) remain the most frequently adopted governance frameworks, while GDPR (11%) and HIPAA (6%) exert substantial influence in European and healthcare contexts. Evidence indicates a growing shift toward automated compliance monitoring, dashboard-based audit management, and cloud-integrated GRC systems, reflecting a convergence of governance, risk, and compliance technologies. Sectoral analysis shows dominance in finance (21.25%), government (18.75%), and corporate-government collaborations (17.5%), with limited yet emerging research in healthcare (6.25%), ICT (7.5%), and SMEs (5%). Despite methodological progress, 61% of studies lacked detailed reporting on implementation models, revealing persistent gaps in transparency, resource adequacy, and sectoral applicability. The findings underscore that structured adoption of international standards enhances risk mitigation, decision efficiency, and regulatory alignment, but implementation barriers-such as system complexity, skill deficits, and limited empirical validation-remain. The review recommends prioritizing leadership capacity-building, evidence-based performance metrics, and cross-sector collaboration to enable adaptive, data-driven governance systems. Future research should expand empirical validation across underrepresented sectors to reinforce evidence-based policy and practical cybersecurity governance design.

title: From Hype to Strategy: Using Extensional Representation Encoding to Evaluate Quantum Computing's Business Value
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) and HSBC Limited

detail.title: From Hype to Strategy: Using Extensional Representation Encoding to Evaluate Quantum Computing's Business Value
detail.abstract: Quantum computing can transform socioeconomic systems, but its complexity creates significant cognitive barriers for firms assessing its value. This study uses a design science approach and applies exaptation to explore how extensional representation encoding can reduce these barriers. We propose a 2x2 extensional representation encoding framework with four encoding paths. Through a qualitative study, we find that encoding classical contextual algorithms into extensional representations is the most effective. However, this process requires technical solutions to translate classical instruction sequences into quantum algorithms. We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) as an example and develop a QMC extensional encoding framework, which treats single-value samples as distribution variables. Validated through the FinQMC artifact in two use cases, the framework shows consistent instruction sequences and accurate encoding through both mathematical proofs and empirical results. Our findings provide actionable strategies for evaluating emerging technologies, offering firms and researchers a practical approach to using extensional representation encoding.

detail.title: Coopetition dynamics in platform-based supply chains: When and with whom to cooperate?

detail.abstract: Platform-based supply chains have become central to modern retail ecosystems, where multi-homing by merchants and customers reshapes competitive dynamics and strategic decision-making. Despite extensive analytical work on pricing, network effects and service investment, prior research has paid limited attention to the logistics dimension of platform-based coopetition, often treating fulfillment and logistics-related determinants as exogenous or uniform. In this study, we ask when and why rival platforms should engage in logistics-oriented coopetition, shifting from price coordination to interface alignment without shared facilities. Using a Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning approach, we identify state-contingent windows in which cooperation emerges endogenously under near-symmetric logistics costs and heightened multi-homing congestion/SLA risk, improving Cost-to-Time Efficiency and lifting profits while leaving market shares broadly stable. The findings reveal that cooperation across platforms can emerge endogenously as a rational equilibrium when logistics cost structures are sufficiently symmetric, network externalities are strong and congestion externalities threaten service reliability. Our study validates the notion that logistics is a strategic axis for selective alignment among rivals, reinforcing the view that operational complementarities, rather than market pooling, underpin economic viability, resilience and consumer welfare.

title: How The Mutual Feedback Between Ranking Algorithms and Individual Choices Affects Digital Platforms' Performance
affiliations: Xidian University, University of Zurich, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) and University of Zurich

detail.title: How The Mutual Feedback Between Ranking Algorithms and Individual Choices Affects Digital Platforms' Performance
detail.abstract: Ranking algorithms are essential components of modern e-commerce platforms, allowing users to rapidly sort the available products and find the products that best suit their needs. In turn, the algorithmic outputs are influenced by the users' actions recorded in the data used to train the algorithms. This behavioral feedback loop affects users' satisfaction, their decisions on whether to use again the platform, and ultimately, the platform's profitability. Yet capturing the feedback effects between these variables has remained elusive so far, which leaves platform managers with scarce theory-backed guidelines to choose which algorithms to deploy. Here we introduce a general-purpose agent-based modeling framework where platform-level performance variables are emergent properties of the entangled human-algorithm dynamics. The proposed framework connects users' purchasing and churning behavior in a generic e-commerce platform with the platform's ranking algorithm, and it could be potentially adapted to model the coupled human-algorithm dynamics in any algorithm-driven platform. We use the resulting agent-based model to provide an extensive back-to-back comparison of collaborative filtering and popularity-based algorithms. We illustrate how the simulations' results can provide managers with a roadmap of the most relevant factors to choose the algorithm that best suits their platform's needs. Finally, we demonstrate how the model can be calibrated with empirical behavioral data, and validate its predictions with newly-collected data from a randomized controlled experiment. The proposed modeling framework could be used by managers to assess ranking algorithms for e-commerce before running potentially costly A/B tests with real customers.

detail.abstract: Rising minimum wages are pressuring labor-intensive service industries-especially foodservice-through escalating personnel costs. "Sales per labor hour" has long served as a managerial efficiency metric; however, overreliance on numeric control risks obscuring the experiential value of service. Building on Service-Dominant Logic (SDL) and integrating the concept of Non-Monetary Experiential Value (NMEV), this paper reframes customers not as passive consumers but as partners in value co-creation. We advance a three-layer framework-Theory-Application-Commons-to synthesize efficiency and added value, economic outcomes and social meaning. The theoretical contribution clarifies a dynamic mechanism: efficiency as Resource Availability, SDL as Resource Integration Support, and NMEV as the Experiential Outcome. An application case ("premium set" menu) demonstrates how share-based menu design enhances simultaneous eating, variety sharing, and social bonding while stabilizing operations. We conclude with implications for public value creation and an agenda for empirical validation.

title: From Threat to Opportunity: How Offline Stores Compete Amid Online-to-Offline Disruption
affiliations: , Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University and Nanyang Technological University - Nanyang Business School

detail.title: From Threat to Opportunity: How Offline Stores Compete Amid Online-to-Offline Disruption
detail.abstract: The rise of digital platforms presents a fundamental trade-off for consumers: the unmatched convenience of online services versus the unique experiential and social value of physical stores. While online-to-offline (O2O) platforms excel in efficiency and cost, they inherently lack the capacity to provide the atmospheric and interactive benefits of offline encounters. This study investigates how this trade-off shapes the competitive landscape for traditional businesses following disruptive O2O entry. Examining the laundry service industry in South Korea, we employ a difference-indifferences approach and causal forest analysis to assess the impact on store survival. We find that O2O entry generally increases the likelihood of store closure, underscoring the power of convenience. However, this effect is not uniform. Stores offering features that reduce perceived waiting time or foster positive emotional experiences, such as internet access and pet-friendly environments, are more resilient. We also test whether positive customer sentiment mediates this effect and find that internet access improves review sentiment after the introduction of O2O, which in turn enhances survival. These findings underscore the importance of leveraging servicescape-driven experiential value as a differentiation strategy that enables offline businesses to remain competitive in digitally transforming service environments.

title: Dynamic Growth Theory: A Resilience-Based Framework for Sustainable Organizational Growth

detail.title: Dynamic Growth Theory: A Resilience-Based Framework for Sustainable Organizational Growth
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Dynamic Growth Theory (DGT) as a comprehensive, resilience-based framework designed to support long-term organizational growth in complex and volatile business environments. DGT is structured around four core principles-Resilience, Constancy and Change (Fueki-Ryūkō), Growth Mindset, and Acceptance of Fate-that, when integrated, create a dynamic and adaptive system for sustainable development. Drawing from psychology, strategic management, and Eastern philosophical traditions, DGT offers an applied methodology for navigating uncertainty, fostering innovation, and embedding long-term competitiveness in sectors such as the food service industry. The framework emphasizes continuous learning, cultural adaptation, and proactive transformation as keys to enduring success.

detail.abstract: Personal branding on LinkedIn has become a critical driver for entrepreneurs, consultants, and professionals seeking visibility, credibility, and lead generation in increasingly competitive digital markets. While numerous guides exist on how to craft posts and build engagement, most approaches remain tactical and fragmented. There is limited research on systematic, innovation-driven methods for solving the recurring contradictions faced by content creators such as balancing frequency with depth, or engagement with credibility. This paper proposes a novel application of TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving) to the domain of LinkedIn personal branding. Originating in engineering and product innovation, TRIZ offers structured principles for resolving contradictions. By adapting these principles, we develop a 13-feature framework that maps key tensions in LinkedIn content (e.g., posting frequency vs. authority, virality vs. niche positioning, authenticity vs. lead generation) to practical, repeatable solutions. Each feature (e.g., Hook First, Post Type, Frameworkization, Mirror ICP, Story Stacking) is further broken down into sub-features and integrated into a tension-resolution matrix (in place of the contradiction-resolution matrix as in the case of TRIZ) tailored for digital branding. Methodologically, this study is conceptual and framework-oriented, drawing on a synthesis of TRIZ theory, digital marketing literature, and practitioner insights. The findings illustrate how TRIZ principles can be repurposed to systematically design LinkedIn content strategies that balance competing goals, ensuring posts are not only engaging but also credible, skimmable, and lead-generating. Practical illustrations and applied scenarios are included to demonstrate usability. The implications of this work are twofold. Theoretically, it extends TRIZ into the field of digital marketing and personal branding, an underexplored area in scholarly research. Practically, it offers entrepreneurs, consultants, and professionals a structured toolkit to innovate in their content creation and resolve contradictions that typically hinder their growth. Limitations include the absence of empirical testing across large datasets; future research should validate this framework through case studies, surveys, or experimental trials. This paper contributes to both academic and practitioner communities by bridging innovation theory and personal branding practice. It demonstrates that TRIZ can serve not only as a tool for engineering design but also as a method for systematically innovating personal branding strategies in the digital era.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to analyze the impact of on-the-job and off-the-job training on improving employee skills and performance growth. It is important to research how training has been studied by different disciplines at different times, what function it is thought to have according to different approaches, as well as how researchers of different times and currents have tried to evaluate it. An employee's performance is a function of ability, motivation, and opportunity to participate, and it can also create a favorable social climate that encourages employees to act in accordance with the firm's objectives (Imani, Foroudi, Seyyedamiri, & Dehghani, 2020). The data used primarily provided by selfadministered questionnaires were used with a sample of 100 respondents with a deliberate sample including employees in the private sector, and those who have been part of on-the-job or off-the-job training. This data from the questionnaires were processed with the IBM SPSS program where the frequencies, crossconstructions, and correlations between the variables were described. Respondents also request to be included in the Training Plan: for "soft skills". Among other things, the findings result in a positive but weak correlation between the selection of the training method and the performance of the employees.

detail.abstract: This study proposes a new approach to mitigating water scarcity in conflict-affected zones through the redesign of local architecture as efficient hydrological infrastructure. We targeted Taiz, Yemen, a war-torn city suffering from drought and deficient water supply, where we designed and piloted geospatially optimized fog-harvesting systems. Applying parametric design and cutting-edge geospatial diagnostics (drawing on Sentinel-1 and CHIRPS datasets), the systems were optimized to provide high environmental and socioeconomic returns. Our in-field data, collected over 18 months, demonstrate a remarkable 98% reduction in water salinity, a superior yield of 654 ± 47 L/day/tower, and satisfied microbial purity (0 CFU/ml E. coli). From an economic standpoint, the system reduces water costs by 97% compared to the traditional method of water transportation, now costing $0.0014/L. This approach develops a reproducible and scalable model for dealing with water-risk resilience in dry zones. The technology's reliance on local materials (volcanic rock, PVA-SiO₂ hydrogel) and human-driven manufacturing and maintenance processes also ensures its scalability and sustainability in the face of adversity. This study contributes a vital paradigm for climate-resilient architecture, geospatial water mapping, and hydro-architectural resilience through the emphasis on nano-enhanced materials and parametric vernacular design.

title: America's Most 'Far-Reaching Institution': The Bureaucratic Work and Legacies of the Freedmen's Bureau *
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Political Science and University of Chicago

detail.title: America's Most 'Far-Reaching Institution': The Bureaucratic Work and Legacies of the Freedmen's Bureau *
detail.abstract: Most policies adopted by states require bureaucracy to implement their provisions. This paper examines how bureaucratic capacity affects policy reach and consequences. Our focus is the US Freedmen's Bureau, a vital component of Reconstruction after the Civil War that exemplified many aspects common to service delivery and bureaucratic administration. Using an original dataset that provides the most comprehensive portrait of the Freedmen's Bureau assembled to date, we link the distribution, organization, and personnel arrangements of Bureau offices to local socioeconomic outcomes. We find that the Freedmen's Bureau had positive effects for both Black and white residents of counties that hosted offices. Moreover, these effects were moderated by office longevity and personnel arrangements. The effects persisted through at least 1940, though the magnitude attenuated for Blacks and increased for whites. The findings suggest the federal government played a larger, and more successful-albeit unequalrole in citizens' lives than commonly believed.

title: COVID-19 Induced Asian Discrimination and Health: What Can We Learn from Reported Health Status?
affiliations: and Agnes Scott College

detail.title: COVID-19 Induced Asian Discrimination and Health: What Can We Learn from Reported Health Status?

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: There is a growing literature that provides concrete evidence of the effects of the pandemic on both health and socioeconomic outcomes. While the general negative effects of the pandemic were felt across race, gender, social status, and age, there is emerging literature suggesting a disproportionate negative effect on people of Asian heritage, referred to by some as an Asian chilling effect. There is documented evidence that the origin of the COVID-19 virus in Asia led to increased discrimination and xenophobia against individuals of Asian descent, which resulted in an unprecedented rise in anti-Asian hate during COVID. In this paper, we estimate the impact of this treatment on reported health status in the U.S. Using a difference-in-differences (DD) approach, we provide evidence that COVID-induced discrimination against Asians led to a chilling effect in the U.S. In particular, we find a decrease in the health status of Asians compared to comparable non-Hispanic Whites from the pandemic onward. Our results are consistent across alternative measures of health. We also conduct multiple tests to ensure the robustness of our results and provide a potential pathway for this effect.

title: The Price of Breaking Up: Wage Shocks and Household Dissolution
affiliations: University of Zaragoza, University of Zaragoza - Department of Economic Analysis and Columbia University - Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics

detail.title: The Price of Breaking Up: Wage Shocks and Household Dissolution

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Household dissolution is a key concern in family economics, with implications for individual welfare, child outcomes, income trajectories, or wealth, which ultimately impact inequality and vulnerability. This paper examines how wage dynamics relate to the stability of dual-earner households, using a collective model with limited commitment, where spouses commit to future behavior subject to individual rationality constraints, allowing for renegotiation of intrahousehold arrangements or household dissolution. We use data from the PSID over 1999-2019, and estimate how spouses wage changes relate to divorce, accounting for observed behaviors, demographics, and unobserved heterogeneity. The results show that large negative wage changes significantly increase the likelihood of divorce, while positive changes have no effect, as the model predicts. This pattern is consistent with asymmetric intrahousehold insurance, highlighting the role of economic risk and bargaining asymmetries in shaping family dynamics, and informs policies targeting household vulnerability to income shocks.

detail.abstract: We study the evolution of the child penalty and gender-related inequality in the Netherlands. We use administrative panel data from 1989 to 2022 in an extension of the event study approach used in Kleven et al. (2019b). We document a substantial decline in child penalties (in earnings) for first-time mothers from 60% in the early 1990s to 35% in the 2010s. This decline is much larger than in the handful of other countries documented so far. However, looking at subperiods, we also find that the decline in the child penalty in the Netherlands has stalled in the mid 2000s, despite a steep rise in spending on formal childcare. Next, we decompose the gender-related inequality for parents into inequality related to children, education, migration background and a residual. We find that overall gender-related inequality and child-related gender inequality decline in parallel over time. The role of education and migration background is small and becomes less important over time. Hence, a substantial residual remains, and cannot be attributed to the aforementioned factors. We also show that the event-time window used is crucial for the contribution of the child penalty to the evolution of gender inequality.

detail.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of major tax reforms in Peru using a Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model calibrated with recent national accounts. Two counterfactual scenarios are analyzed. In Counterfactual 1 (Law No. 32387 on municipal transfers), productive effects are modest: private investment declines while local public investment rises, highlighting the reform's redistributive but weakly growth-inducing nature. In Counterfactual 2 (the New Agrarian Law), tax incentives stimulate value-added and exports in agriculture and agroindustry, generating spillover effects in related sectors such as fisheries and forestry. However, this expansion comes at the expense of public investment and non-prioritized industries, revealing a reallocation of resources toward favored activities. Overall, the findings demonstrate the value of CGE models in identifying redistributive trade-offs across sectors and agents, providing important insights into the broader consequences of fiscal policy reforms.

title: Beyond Collective Agreements: The Rise of the Wage Cushion in Germany

detail.title: Beyond Collective Agreements: The Rise of the Wage Cushion in Germany

detail.abstract: Representative establishment data reveal that over 60 percent of German plants covered by collective agreements pay wages above the level stipulated in the agreements, creating a wage cushion between actual and contractual wages. While collective bargaining coverage has fallen over time, the prevalence of wage cushions has increased, particularly in eastern Germany. Cross-sectional and fixed-effects analyses for 2008-2023 indicate that in western Germany the presence of a wage cushion is mainly related to plant profitability, unemployment, vacancies, and the business cycle. Plants which apply collective agreements at the firm rather than the sectoral level are less likely to have wage cushions since firm-level agreements make it easier to explicitly take firm-specific conditions into account. In eastern Germany, however, the explanatory power of these variables is considerably lower. Against the backdrop of falling bargaining coverage, the increasing prevalence of wage cushions suggests that the traditionally rigid German system of wage determination has become more flexible and differentiated.

title: Digital Innovation as a Bank Risk Mitigator: Empirical Insights from Chinese Commercial Banks

detail.abstract: The rapid spread of digital technologies has led traditional banks, long-standing pillars of the financial sector, to embrace digital innovation. This study investigates how digital innovation influences bank risk. We develop a new hand-collected index that captures five dimensions of digital innovation, namely volume, variety, agency, generativity, and convergence. Using a panel of 391 Chinese commercial banks from 2009 to 2018, we find that banks with higher levels of digital innovation tend to engage in less excessive risk-taking. This negative relationship is robust across multiple identification strategies, including difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, Heckman two-stage estimation, and change-on-change regressions, which address concerns of endogeneity. Two mechanisms explain this effect. First, digital innovation strengthens market discipline by improving bank transparency. Second, it enhances market power by improving loan quality and reducing information asymmetries between banks and borrowers. The bank stabilizing effect also varies across different dimensions and strategic goals of digital innovation. In addition, the risk-reducing effect is more pronounced for banks located in provinces with greater digital innovation by other financial service providers, for non–state-owned banks, for banks lacking national geographic reach, and for those in provinces with stronger legal enforcement or more developed credit markets. These findings highlight the strategic role of digital innovation in shaping bank risk and provide important implications for managers, regulators, and other stakeholders concerned with financial stability.

detail.abstract: We analyze the second-price all-pay auction under mean-variance preferences. We characterize the variance-averse Nash equilibrium bidding strategy with valuations of general distributions, which is consistently lower than the risk-neutral Nash equilibrium bidding strategy. We show that the varianceaverse Nash equilibrium bidding strategy in second-price all-pay auctions is consistently higher than that in first-price all-pay auctions. We establish that the variance-averse Nash equilibrium bidding strategy declines with the variance aversion parameter and the count of bidders, respectively. Additionally, we find that the seller's revenue expectation and variance decline with the variance aversion parameter, respectively. In the extended model, we discuss the variance-averse Nash equilibrium bidding strategy that accommodates bidders facing two independent exogenous shocks, and find that the exogenous shocks to valuations lead to more conservative bids, while the exogenous shocks to cost of failure induce more aggressive bids. We discuss the variance-averse Nash equilibrium bidding strategy under meanvariance preferences in general form, focusing on equilibrium existence and its comparative properties to those established under mean-variance preferences in linear form.

title: Golden CAPM
affiliations: University of Neuchatel and University of Neuchatel

detail.title: Golden CAPM
detail.abstract: When asset returns are measured in ounces of gold rather than U.S. dollars, the Sharpe-Lintner Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) holds. We empirically test this by regressing asset returns onto market betas estimated using gold-denominated series. Estimated intercepts are economically small and statistically indistinguishable from zero, implying that the golden CAPM successfully explains the crosssection of expected returns. Moreover, the regression slopes are statistically significant and indistinguishable from the average market returns. We show that denominating returns in ounces of gold improves the explanatory power of all multi-factor models such as Fama-French three-, five-, and six-factor models, and Carhart fourfactor model. Yet, across all model-test asset combinations, none outperforms the simple golden CAPM applied to beta-sorted portfolios.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in high-stakes areas such as climate policy, health resource allocation, and conflict resolution. The introduction of quantum computing into AI creates both new opportunities and new ethical challenges, as larger solution spaces can produce innovative outcomes along with hidden trade-offs. This paper presents a framework that combines Vedic ethical principles including Rta (cosmic order), Dharma (context-sensitive duty), and Ahimsa (non-harm) with quantum-enhanced AI to guide complex policy decisions. It introduces the Quantum Ethical Uncertainty (QEU) metric, which measures ethical ambiguity in quantum-AI decision spaces. The framework also develops entangled ethics models inspired by Indra’s Net, quantum compassion algorithms for proactive harm analysis, and quantum karma simulations for examining long-term consequences. Simulated case studies in climate adaptation and conflict resolution show that this approach expands the range of policy options while identifying ethical risks that conventional assessments overlook. The findings suggest that integrating quantum-enhanced AI with culturally grounded ethics can improve fairness and resilience in policy contexts while highlighting the importance of empirical testing and adaptation to diverse cultural settings.

detail.abstract: We study cointegration in matrix--valued time series, where variables are naturally organized along two interacting margins (e.g., countries x indicators or portfolios x characteristics). The econometric literature proposed two competing reduced rank specifications: the matrix error correction model (MECM) and the cointegrated matrix Auto-Regressive model (ECC–MAR). Our first contribution is analytical: we derive explicit moving–average representations for both models, which disentangle the permanent component---spanned by common stochastic trends---from the transitory component, clarifying how left– and right–side cointegration spaces propagate shocks. Second, we establish a sharp diagnostic: under ECC–MAR each row and each column of Xt are cointegrated with a positive and common margin rank, while under MECM individual rows and columns are not cointegrated. This yields a simple identification procedure based on the Johansen test on rows and columns to distinguish between MECM and ECC–MAR prior to estimation. Monte Carlo experiments document accurate size and power properties of the diagnostic.

title: The Africonomics Theory of Economic Cycles: A Natural-Moral Framework for Boom-Bust Dynamics
affiliations: Afrindependent Institute

detail.title: The Africonomics Theory of Economic Cycles: A Natural-Moral Framework for Boom-Bust Dynamics
detail.abstract: The Africonomics Theory of Economic Cycles (ATEC) presents a natural-moral framework for understanding one of the most destructive phenomena in modern economies: recurring boom-bust cycles. While traditional economic theories view these cycles as natural fluctuations within market economies, Africonomics demonstrates that they are not natural market phenomena, but rather a structural injustice caused by fiat monetary manipulation—artificial credit creation and interest rate suppression that enriches elites while impoverishing the majority. By distorting interest rates, misallocating capital, and incentivizing speculative investment, fiat monetary systems instigate artificial expansions that inevitably collapse into recessions or depressions—causing widespread instability and impoverishment. Through historical and contemporary case studies, including the Mississippi Bubble, the Dot-com and subprime mortgage crises, and the Angolan debt-fueled downturn, this paper reveals that fiat monetary systems generate recurring boom-bust cycles and chronic instability. Africonomics also offers a principled framework for ending these destructive cycles through the establishment of sound money and honest credit grounded in natural-moral law.

title: The Impact of E-Commerce Adoption on Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises Performance in Rural Areas: Evidence from Indonesia

detail.title: The Impact of E-Commerce Adoption on Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises Performance in Rural Areas: Evidence from Indonesia
detail.abstract: E-commerce has transformed global business operations, but its adoption varies due to differences in digital infrastructure and economic development. While e-commerce has thrived in developed areas, rural areas still face challenges. In rural Indonesia, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are increasingly embracing e-commerce, but the specific impact on their business performance has not been thoroughly studied. This research investigates how e-commerce adoption, through platforms, social media, and websites, influences the performance of MSMEs in rural Indonesia. Specifically, the study evaluates whether e-commerce adoption affects rural MSMEs' employment, revenue, costs, profit, and productivity. Using individual MSME data collected by the Central Bank of Indonesia and employing the Inverse Probability Weighted Regression Adjustment (IPWRA) method, the findings show that e-commerce adoption, especially through social media, has significantly enhanced profitability. However, this adoption has also led to increased operational costs. The impact of e-commerce varies depending on business size, location, and owner characteristics such as education and age. The study emphasizes the importance of prioritizing social media to drive profitability while being mindful of the associated digitalization costs. Furthermore, the study results provide compelling evidence for enhancing digital infrastructure and offering financial support to rural MSMEs to help them fully leverage the benefits of e-commerce.

title: Do Activist Hedge Funds Care About ESG?
affiliations: and Technical University of Darmstadt

detail.title: Do Activist Hedge Funds Care About ESG?
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between activist hedge fund (AHF) targeting and corporate environmental and social performance (ESP). Using U.S. data from 2010 to 2022, we propose and test an ESG-indifference hypothesis, arguing that AHFs prioritize financial objectives while largely disregarding ESP considerations. Consistent with this view, we find no significant relationship between ESP and the likelihood of AHF targeting. Analyses of posttargeting effects reveal that AHF engagements significantly impede the development of target firms' ESP relative to matched peers. Negative effects are evident across the environmental and social pillars and are concentrated in emissions reduction, resource use, workforce practices, and human rights, while other areas remain unaffected. We argue that the affected areas are closely tied to short-term financial pressures, suggesting that deteriorations in ESP are incidental rather than deliberate. To explain this pattern, we propose and test managerial attention shifts and operational value focus as two mechanisms that drive the effect on ESP, providing further evidence in support of the ESG-indifference hypothesis. Our results underscore the trade-off between shareholder value creation and corporate sustainability under hedge fund activism and provide novel evidence that activists remain largely indifferent to ESG considerations in both target selection and post-engagement outcomes.

title: Systems Analysis and Peacebuilding: A Conceptual Stock-Taking and Forward Research Agenda
affiliations: University of Oslo and University of Oslo - Centre for Development and the Environment

detail.title: Systems Analysis and Peacebuilding: A Conceptual Stock-Taking and Forward Research Agenda
detail.abstract: The growing complexity of armed conflicts has prompted the expansion of conceptual frameworks to better understand their multifaceted and interconnected nature. Systems thinking has emerged as an increasingly popular approach in peacebuilding in response to this need. This approach leverages peacebuilding's "local turn" to promise a deeper study of complex social systems and the interplay among social, economic, political, and cultural factors. But what is "systems thinking", and what does its proliferation mean for peacebuilding scholarship today? To answer, this conceptual review systematically catalogues the most relevant 250 scholarly articles on systems thinking and analysis, identifying how systems thinking in peacebuilding is typically discussed. We then build a framework for four interconnected ways that systems thinking is commonly framed: as heuristic, diagnostic, process-oriented, and adaptive approaches. Our framework strengthens our knowledge about how systems thinking is used in peacebuilding research and practice, and where its conceptual strengths and weaknesses may lie. We conclude with a discussion of how a deeper critical analysis of the "systems turn" in peacebuilding scholarship and the use of systems as a way to study complex conflict is warranted.

detail.abstract: This study employs textual analysis of earnings conference calls to explore how firms adjust their capital structures in response to increased supply chain risk. We find a negative and statistically significant relationship between supply chain risk and financial leverage, with the effect primarily explained through the cash flow volatility and the cost of debt channels. Furthermore, the negative impact of supply chain risk on leverage is more pronounced for firms with lower revenue diversification, less vertical integration, and fewer financial constraints. Overall, our findings support the notion that firms facing increased threats from supply chain disruptions are motivated to adopt a more conservative capital structure by reducing their financial leverage.

title: Does Self-Employment Pay? The Role of Voluntary Mobility and Timing
affiliations: U.S. Census Bureau

detail.title: Does Self-Employment Pay? The Role of Voluntary Mobility and Timing
detail.abstract: In this paper, I reexamine the earnings differential between self-and wage-employed men. Previous analysts have consistently concluded that self-employment does not pay, but this result is puzzling, in part, because self-employed men work longer hours and bear more income risk than do their wage-employed counterparts. Using data from the 1979 National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, I find that the timing and (voluntary or involuntary) nature of men's transitions into new self-employed jobs are important determinants of whether they receive wage gains. I find that when a man transitions from wage-employment to a new self-employed job voluntarily and early in his career, his wage is predicted to increase contemporaneously by 31%. The magnitude of this increase is 2.6 times larger than the predicted wage gain associated with a voluntary, early career transition to a new wage job. Conversely, I find that when a man transitions from wage-employment to a new self-employed job involuntarily and late in his career, his wage is predicted to decrease contemporaneously by 18%. The magnitude of this decrease is larger than the predicted 13% wage decrease associated with an involuntary, late career transition to a new wage job.

detail.abstract: A successful green transition requires aligning electricity demand with renewable supply, which variable pricing can achieve. We use novel high-frequency data on electricity consumption and an instrumental variable approach to analyze electricity price responsiveness of Danish households. We estimate electricity price elasticities across and within days. We find that higher prices lead households to adjust their consumption, mostly through level decreases rather than shifting use to cheaper off-peak hours. The level cuts persist after prices fall, especially for lower-income households, while within-day shifting is modest and concentrated among higher-income households.

title: Navigating Politics, Culture, and Markets: The Case of "Careem"

detail.title: Navigating Politics, Culture, and Markets: The Case of "Careem"
detail.abstract: This paper applies the PESTLE framework to the case of Careem, a ride-hailing company founded in Dubai in 2012 and later acquired by Uber. The study investigates the political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental conditions that shaped Careem's rapid rise in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Political restrictions initially prevented the firm from establishing operations in Saudi Arabia, pushing its founders to set up the business in the United Arab Emirates, where regulations were more favourable to foreign entrepreneurs. Economically, Careem benefited from unmet demand, particularly in Saudi Arabia, where women were not permitted to drive until 2018. Socially, the company redefined the taxi profession and improved safety perceptions for both drivers and passengers. Technological challenges included building reliable GPS and billing systems, while legally, operating across 14 jurisdictions required constant adaptation. Environmentally, weak mapping infrastructure and cultural skepticism towards start-ups created further hurdles. Despite these challenges, Careem established itself as a regional leader, ultimately being acquired by Uber for $3.1 billion. This analysis highlights how context-specific adaptation is critical for success in emerging markets and how the PESTLE framework can illuminate the interplay between structural conditions and entrepreneurial strategy.

detail.abstract: Most biologic drugs are administered in clinics rather than dispensed by pharmacies. This structure magnifies the significance of the vertical relationships between clinics and the large multi-product firms that commercialize the drugs. We study how the strength of these relationships influences the market penetration of biosimilars-lower-cost copies of reference biologic drugs. Our evidence reveals a turf war-type dynamic in which the makers of reference and biosimilar products compete for exclusive product assortment leveraging their broader commercial relationships with clinics. These findings imply that the competitive dynamics in biosimilar markets differ fundamentally from those for drugs dispensed by community pharmacies. Our results also suggest that biosimilar innovation and uptake may hinge on whether firms possess the commercial capabilities to effectively engage in the turf war.

title: Police Surveillance And The Perils Of Techno-Solutionism
affiliations: UC Law, San Francisco

detail.title: Police Surveillance And The Perils Of Techno-Solutionism
detail.abstract:
This Article reveals how the expansion of surveillance technology into local law enforcement, while intended to solve perceived staffing challenges, has remolded the purposes of policing. It has reoriented policing from evidence gathering and deterrence to a focus on constant data collection and crime prediction. Law enforcement's embrace of surveillance technology constitutes a form of techno-solutionism, a concept originating in urban planning and philosophy of technology and applied here to policing. It is the view that all complex social situations can be simplified to measurable data primed for quick-fix technical answers. This Article argues that, while technology may have been adopted by police to respond to a specific problem, it has also changed the problem itself and altered the array of potential solutions, which often requires ever more technology. Far from being a neutral or passive tool, technology acts as an agent with its own orientation and momentum. In this way, technology has altered the ultimate goals of policing. 

Law enforcement's turn to surveillance technology as a tool to address staffing challenges -- a "force multiplier" promising increased efficiency in meeting policing goals with fewer officers -- is an example of a larger techno-solutionist trend in American policing. This current emerged in the backlash to the Civil Rights movement in the late 1960s and has continued through the War on Terror to the current moment. The expansion of police surveillance in the last fifty years, in general, and its techno-solutionist trajectory, in particular, lead to troubling implications about how surveillance technology will deepen racial bias and other inequities in policing.

detail.abstract: This paper aims to examine the impact of the Russia-Ukraine war on the performance of the Group of Twenty (G20) countries by analyzing the economic performance of these countries before and after the war, analyzing and measuring empirically from 2000 to 2022. The Russian invasion of Ukraine has prompted many researchers to study the impact of the conflict on the economic performance of the world’s most prosperous countries. Furthermore, the influence of global commerce has demonstrated that the Russia-Ukraine war has impacted the global trade imbalance, harming the economic performance of the 27 European Union (EU) nations (Misini & Tosuni, 2023b). The methodology is based on a comparison of each of the G20 country’s economic performance indexes (EPIs) to the countries of the EU. These countries’ performance will be evaluated using the most essential macroeconomic indicators: unemployment, inflation, fiscal deficit, and yearly economic growth. In addition, this paper will examine the influence of the Russia-Ukraine war on the economic performance of these countries (G20). The analysis employed dot plot analysis, descriptive statistical analysis, and regression to conduct a more scientific investigation. The findings reveal that nations with high inflation as a result of the Russia-Ukraine war had lower economic performance, while those with low inflation had higher economic performance. Countries with lower inflation have produced greater economic results. Turkey and Argentina have experienced significant swings in economic performance. Economic growth and the budget deficit have had a favorable impact on the G20 countries’ economic performance.

detail.abstract: Self-acting "shopping agents" are no longer science fiction. Deployed by major platforms like Google, Amazon, and Walmart, AI systems are evolving from passive advisors to autonomous decision-makers capable of opening accounts, canceling subscriptions, and finalizing purchases without human oversight. Though AI shopping agents have the potential to improve consumer satisfaction and marketplace competition, shopping agents come with attendant risks. By foregrounding shopping's overlooked economic, psychological, and cultural stakes, we reframe the rise of AI agents as a critical challenge for the law and society, rather than a mere evolution in retail convenience. Drawing on sociology, marketing, and behavioral science research, we demonstrate how AI delegation will fundamentally reshape consumer markets by optimizing purchases while potentially consolidating corporate power, diminishing consumer agency, and eroding social connection. Traditional legal doctrines-built on assumptions of human deliberation-are structurally misaligned with algorithmic commerce. To address these gaps, we propose a machine-aware regulatory toolkit featuring "algorithmic nutrition labels," design nudges for preserving shopper self-determination, and structural safeguards, including age limits and sunset provisions. Without rapid legal intervention, algorithmic commerce threatens to undermine the economic discipline, personal autonomy, and social connections that give shopping meaning beyond mere acquisition.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Specttro's Paradigm, a novel framework integrating game theory, behavioral economics, network effects, and AI-driven simulations to transform competitive strategy analysis. By addressing the limitations of static, siloed models rooted in perfect rationality, the paradigm enables a shift from zero-sum competition to collaborative, positive-sum value creation. We formalize the composite utility function of the paradigm, which represents a stable strategic outcome where players optimize utilities that account for rational expectations, cognitive biases, interconnected values, and adaptive simulations. The central theoretical contribution of this paper is a mathematical proof of the existence and uniqueness of this equilibrium. We establish existence using the Debreu-Glicksberg-Fan fixed-point theorem and uniqueness from the properties of strictly concave games. We further prove that this equilibrium yields a weak Pareto improvement over baseline models, satisfying the positive-sum paradigm ethos. The paradigm's dynamic adaptability and ethical AI governance offer actionable insights for academia and practice, redefining strategic decision-making in complex, interconnected markets.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal impact of education on volunteering participation (intensive margin) and frequency (extensive margin) among older adults, using crosscountry panel data from the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) for the period 2013-2019. We employ compulsory schooling as an instrumental variable for education. The results show that each additional year of education increases the probability of volunteering participation by 6.8 percentage points and raises volunteering frequency by 11.9 percentage points. Furthermore, the results of our heterogeneity analysis indicate that education has a positive impact on volunteering in collectivistic countries, but the opposite is true for individualistic countries. We also find that the impact is most pronounced among individuals aged 50-64 for volunteering participation while it is negative for volunteering frequency, with diminishing returns among older age groups.

detail.title: The Value(s) of Women Artists
detail.abstract: I use data on values to challenge the belief that women produce art of lower value. Using data on individuals' occupations in the European Social Survey (ESS) and OLS regressions, I show that women are more likely to be artists in more gender-equal countries. This evidence is consistent with greater barriers to artistic careers for women than men. Using data on Schwartz human values in the ESS, I then show that women artists appear more exceptional in their artistic values than men. My evidence highlights the dangers of equating price with value and reinforces the benefits of continuing to invest in women's art and women artists.

detail.abstract: While social networks influence economic outcomes, the role of the quality of connections is less explored. Using jati-level network data from a unique household survey conducted around India’s first Covid-19 lockdown, we examine how influential caste ties affect distress borrowing. Using randomized caste-based quotas in village elections for causal identification, we find that having an influential caste connection increases household borrowing by 1.34 standard deviations (≈|47,000), nearly double the average borrowing. This effect operates through both intensive and extensive margins: connected individuals borrow more from friends/family and are more likely to access credit from formal sources like banks or cooperatives.

detail.abstract: Economic landscape of Pakistan is determined by an extremely complex interaction of domestic and global forces; navigating it successfully requires a clear understanding of its character. The paper explores the dynamic relationships between macroeconomic variables and GDP growth in Pakistan using the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model and other stability tests using time series data from 1980 to 2022. The analysis includes variables representing GDP per capita, inflation, imports, total debt as a percentage of GDP, total population, and forestry and agricultural output. The correlation matrix shows a positive association between GDP growth rate and GDP per capita, total debt service is inversely correlated with total population, and GDP demonstrates a significant negative correlation. The ARDL results indicate that GDP per capita and the agriculture and forestry sectors are significant drivers of economic growth. Over the period in question, inflation only marginally affected GDP growth showing how important it is to maintain price stability through effective policies. Imports provide short-term benefits by enhancing productivity through capital goods and technology inflows but they may pose long-term challenges due to trade imbalances. The influence of population growth appears to be ambivalent: in the short term it contributes to economic growth by increasing labor supply and consumption; in the long term, however, its effect may become detrimental owing to resource constraints. Public debt shows little influence in the short term but negatively impacts growth over time by increasing the fiscal burden of debt servicing. These findings suggest that to achieve long-term economic stability and growth, the country needs targeted policy interventions that should help it control inflation, manage the debt sustainably, optimize imports, and invest in agriculture, which is an important determinant of GDP growth. Future research should concentrate on sector-specific studies and the effects of political stability on economic growth in order to provide deeper insights contributing to Pakistan’s sustainable economic development.

title: Future Causes of the 2025 Punjab Floods and the Likely Effects on the Indian Economy

detail.title: Future Causes of the 2025 Punjab Floods and the Likely Effects on the Indian Economy
detail.abstract: In late August 2025, the state of Punjab experienced devastating floods that drowned thousands of villages and hundreds of thousands of hectares of agricultural land due to abnormally intense rains, flooded rivers, and ruptured embankments. This paper asks two interconnected questions: (1) what are the future causes likely to cause similar or more severe flood events in Punjab in the future, and (2) how such events will ripple through and impact the entire Indian economy? Based on recent news, peer-reviewed climate science, and economic reasoning, I argue that future flood risk in Punjab will be forced by interacting climate drivers (increasing extreme precipitation associated with anthropogenic warming and changing circulation patterns), upstream hydrological management (dam releases and reservoir operations), and land-use/river management failures (siltation, embankment vulnerabilities, loss of floodplains). The economic effects will be multi-sectoral and persistent: short-term agricultural losses and food-price shocks; agro-supply chain bottlenecks and textiles; fiscal pressures on state and central government budgets; insurance and credit losses; localized disruptions to labour markets and migration; and non-trivial negative impact on short-term GDP growth and long-term productivity in the affected areas. The paper concludes with policy suggestions that minimize both hazard and economic exposure.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of green bond issuance on the yield spreads of conventional bonds in China. Using a sample of 1,468 corporate bonds and a difference-in-differences methodology, we document a significantly persistent reduction of 21 basis points in the yield spreads of existing conventional bonds after the green bond issuance. Our findings support a risk-based explanation: green bond issuance mitigates the environmental regulatory risks faced by the issuer, thereby reducing the perceived default risk of its conventional bonds. These results highlight the broader financial implications of green bond issuance, extending beyond the direct environmental benefits to influence the pricing and risk profile of conventional debt instruments.

detail.abstract: In a 2024 post, we showed that interdealer trading in benchmark U.S. Treasury notes and bonds concentrates on the last trading day of the month, likely due to passive investment funds’ turn-of-month portfolio rebalancing. In this post, we extend our trading activity analysis to the full range of Treasury securities and market segments. title: Voter Myopia in Autocracies: Why Do Citizens Support Short-Term Economic Pain for Long-Term Gains?

detail.title: Voter Myopia in Autocracies: Why Do Citizens Support Short-Term Economic Pain for Long-Term Gains?
detail.abstract: Especially in autocracies, this essay examines voter myopia-that is, the tendency of people to give short-term rewards over long-term ones priority. Under such systems, dictators use this prejudice by providing immediate material benefits to loyal areas, controlling information, and silencing opposing views. The article examines how psychological biases, elite co-optation, and propaganda help to lead voters to tolerate short-term financial suffering in return for the hope of future advantages. Using empirical examples, including social welfare initiatives in electoral autocracies, the study finds that while myopia helps autocratic stability, it runs the danger of collapse if long-term promises are not realized. Voter myopia refers to the tendency of voters to emphasize short-term outcomes over long-term ones because of psychological biases, limited knowledge, emotional factors, and discounting of the future. Human psychology inclines people to prefer immediate rewards; distant benefits are uncertain and thus discounted heavily. In autocracies, this dynamic becomes more pronounced: autocrats, wielding near-complete authority, can manipulate incentives and information in ways that deepen this short-term focus among citizens.

detail.abstract: The purpose of the study on which this article reports was to elaborate on career trajectories of academics in Kosovo. Particular attention is given to efforts to follow international benchmarks such as the Bologna Process at key stages of Kosovo's historical and political development in the last three decades. In this qualitative study, semi-structured interviews were carried out with eleven academics with and without management experience as well as administrators. Findings revealed that Kosovo's higher education system is characterised by a weak organisational culture and an orientation towards externally driven change. Also, we found that academics perceived their role narrowly. The findings suggest that while higher education in Kosovo has moved towards adopting international benchmarks, the identity of the academics has not evolved in parallel to support the transition. A managerialist approach catalysed by the Bologna Process has helped a transition process in higher education in Kosovo. Finally, we propose that for a context in transition, local meaning-making processes for policy transfer are needed. Moving forward, institutional development should be led by academic managers and should serve the professionalisation of academics in Kosovo.

detail.abstract: Climate change poses a significant risk to financial stability by impacting sovereign credit risk. Quantifying the exact impact is difficult as climate risk encompasses different components– transition risk and physical risk – with some of these, as well as the policies to address them, playing out over a long time horizon. In this paper, we use a large panel of 52 developed and developing economies over two decades to empirically investigate the extent to which climate risks influence sovereign yields. The results of a panel regression analysis show that transition risk is associated with higher sovereign yields, with the effect more pronounced for developing economies and for high-emitting countries after the Paris agreement. In contrast, high-temperature anomalies do not appear to be priced-in sovereign borrowing costs. At the same time, countries with high levels of debt tend to record higher sovereign yields as acute physical risk increases. In the medium term, using local projections, we find that sovereign yields respond significantly but also differently to different types of disaster caused by climate change. We also explore the nonlinear effects of weather-related natural disasters on sovereign yields and find a striking contrast in the impact of climate shocks on sovereign borrowing costs according to income level and fiscal space when the shock hits.

detail.abstract: Research on teacher well-being that works from a localized socioeconomic perspective tends to neglect the nestedness of teacher well-being within wider systems. Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) are illustrative of such decontextualised ontological and epistemological foundations. In this article, we demonstrate the benefits of a system dynamics Cultural Political Economy informed analysis for research on teacher well-being in protracted crises. Zooming into teacher contract and salary policies in the Democratic Republic of Congo, we compare our 2 largely qualitative research with two RCTs. Our article yields two insights for future systemic analyses of teacher well-being in protracted crises. First, such research necessitates a methodological design which captures the multiscalar systems in which teacher well-being is embedded. Second, such research requires an exploration of cultural, political and economic dynamics that affect teachers and establish boundaries for teacher well-being.

title: Beyond the Average: Distributional Causal Inference under Imperfect Compliance

detail.title: Beyond the Average: Distributional Causal Inference under Imperfect Compliance
detail.abstract: We study the estimation of distributional treatment effects in randomized experiments with imperfect compliance. When participants do not adhere to their assigned treatments, we leverage treatment assignment as an instrumental variable to identify the local distributional treatment effect-the difference in outcome distributions between treatment and control groups for the subpopulation of compliers. We propose a regression-adjusted estimator based on a distribution regression framework with Neyman-orthogonal moment conditions, enabling robustness and flexibility with high-dimensional covariates. Our approach accommodates continuous, discrete, and mixed discrete-continuous outcomes, and applies under a broad class of covariate-adaptive randomization schemes, including stratified block designs and simple random sampling. We derive the estimator's asymptotic distribution and show that it achieves the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulation results demonstrate favorable finite-sample performance, and we demonstrate the method's practical relevance in an application to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment.

title: Global Care Chains: Everyday Infrastructures of Extractive Constitutionalism

detail.title: Global Care Chains: Everyday Infrastructures of Extractive Constitutionalism
detail.abstract: This article examines global care chains as a translocal and transnational dimension of extractive constitutionalism. Drawing on original data and ethnographic research in Tumaco-a historically semi-rural marginalised Afro-Colombian territory on Colombia's Pacific coast-we follow the intergenerational care labour of Nelly, a grandmother raising her grandchildren while her daughters migrate for domestic work to Colombian cities and abroad. Nelly's story reveals how reproductive labour sustains life amid legal abandonment and economic dispossession. We argue that Latin American constitutionalism, despite its transformative aspirations, actively enables care extractivism. Rights-based frameworks continue to privilege urban, formalised forms of care while marginalising racialised, rural, and communal labour. Even where care is nominally recognised as a right, constitutional orders render the labour of women like Nelly invisible, facilitating its informalisation and subordination within global circuits of accumulation. Engaging feminist political economy and legal theory, we offer a materialist critique of constitutionalism-one that treats care not as a moral ideal or private duty but as an everyday infrastructure of extraction. From Colombia's Pacific periphery, we show how constitutional orders depend on juridically erased care work to reproduce economic and political life, revealing care as central to the architecture of global inequality.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a behavioral-economic model of COVID-19 contagion in Brazil, incorporating the role of President Jair Bolsonaro's public speeches and appearances as informational shocks and behavioral incentives. The model formalizes the interaction among seven key elements: (1) political leadership, (2) contagion rate, (3) total population, (4) infected population, (5) vaccination, (6) denialism, and (7) mortality. It demonstrates that denialism operates as a multiplier of negative externalities, shifting the epidemiological equilibrium and increasing the socially inefficient mortality rate. The theoretical framework is empirically tested using a dynamic panel model with data from Brazil's 27 states between 2020 and 2022. Results indicate that political denialism significantly raised the effective contagion rate, while vaccination and public information campaigns reduced it. The findings provide quantitative evidence that misinformation and political communication shocks can propagate collective behavioral responses with substantial welfare costs.

detail.abstract: The IMF working paper, “Good Supervision: lessons from the field,” examines the effectiveness of On-site Inspections (OSIs) as a supervisory tool in advanced economies (AEs), drawing insights from 60 Basel Core Principles (BCPs) assessments conducted between 2012 and June 2023. Despite their critical role in ensuring financial stability, OSIs are identified as the second-largest weakness among supervisory techniques in AEs. The study highlights challenges such as limited supervisory resources, infrequent inspections of smaller banks, and an over-reliance on off-site monitoring, which cannot fully substitute the insights gained from in-person supervision. Key deficiencies include gaps in OSI scope, frequency, staffing, and enforcement mechanisms, as well as communication and structural issues. The paper underscores the need for supervisory authorities to balance on-site and off-site methods, enhance staffing and inspection practices, and strengthen enforcement capabilities. These improvements are deemed essential to align supervisory practices with BCP standards and foster a more resilient financial system.
